L7@P0: Typical lots of egg yolk phosphatidylcholine have fatty
L8@P0: acid contents of approximately 33% 16:0 (palmitic),
L9@P0: 13% 18:0 (stearic), 31% 18:1(oleic), and 15% 18:2
L10@P0: (linoleic) (other fatty acids being minor contributors),
L11@P0: which would give an average molecular weight of
L12@P0: approximately 768.
L13@P0: The crystalline transition temperature (gel-to-liquid) for
L14@P0: phosphatidylcholine from egg is -15 °C for the heating
L15@P0: curve and -7 °C for the cooling curve.1,2
L16@P0: Product No. P 3556 is suppled as a lyophilized
L17@P0: powder. The same product is available as a solution
L18@P0: in chloroform as Product No. P 2772
L19@P0: Phosphatidylcholine is the major membrane
L20@P0: phospholipid in eukaryotic cells. In addition to being
L21@P0: the major structural component of cellular membranes,
L22@P0: phosphatidylcholine serves as a reservoir for several
L23@P0: lipid messengers. It is the source of the bioactive lipids
L24@P0: lysophosphatidylcholine, phosphatidic acid,
L25@P0: diacylglycerol, lysophosphatidylcholine, plateletactivating factor, and arachidonic acid.3
L26@P0:  An
L27@P0: understanding of the control and regulation of the
L28@P0: several metabolic pathways involved in the formation
L29@P0: of these bioactive lipids is an ongoing science.
L30@P0: Phosphatidylcholine is used for preparation of vesicle
L31@P0: suspensions commonly called liposomes or as
L32@P0: monolayers. There have been several books
L33@P0: published on liposomes and their applications.4,5
L34@P0: Monolayers have been formed using a solution of 1%
L35@P0: soybean phosphatidylcholine in hexane.6
L36@P0: Valinomycin induced changes in membrane potentials
L37@P0: of red blood cell and phospholipid
L38@P0: (phosphatidylcholine from egg yolk plus cholesterol)
L39@P0: vesicle suspensions have been measured using
L40@P0: positively-charged, cyanine dyes that fluorimetrically
L41@P0: responded to the change in potential.7
L42@P0: Purified rhodopsin has been incorporated into soybean
L43@P0: phosphatidylcholine vesicles.8
L44@P0: A procedure for determination of the amount of
L45@P0: oxidation of egg phosphatidylcholine in a liposome
L46@P0: preparation by measurement of the oxidation index
L47@P0: has been published.9
L48@P0:  The oxidation index is the ratio
L49@P0: of the absorbance at 233 nm to the absorbance at
L50@P0: 215 nm. The latter wavelength was chosen since there
L51@P0: is little contribution of the fatty acid carbonyl to the
L52@P0: absorbance at this wavelength, allowing Beer's Law to
L53@P0: be followed. A method of determining choline content
L54@P0: has been published.10
L55@P0: Phosphatidylcholine is purified by a modification of the
L56@P0: chromatography method of Singleton by passing an
L57@P0: extract of egg yolk through an alumina column.11
L58@P0: Precautions and Disclaimer
L59@P0: For Laboratory Use Only. Not for drug, household or
L60@P0: other uses.
L61@P0: Preparation Instructions
L62@P0: Purified egg L-α-phosphatidylcholine is soluble
L63@P0: (100 mg/ml) at room temperatue in chloroform,

L65@P0: solubility characteristics should generally apply to
L66@P0: other purified natural product phosphatidylcholine
L67@P0: products such as from egg, soybean, and brain that
L68@P0: contain unsaturated fatty acids.
